name: Bouncer — meeting-bot control and consent evidence for regulated firms
one_liner: For the CCO or ops lead at a 5-50 person SEC-registered RIA, Bouncer watches every client video meeting across Google Meet and Zoom, tells you which AI notetaker bot joined (yours, the client's, or an unapproved one), captures the consent moment, and produces a per-meeting, exam-ready evidence record the firm can hand an examiner.
problem: AI notetaker bots now join a third of workplace meetings and frequently arrive via an external guest's calendar app, not the host's. For an RIA, each recorded client call is potentially a business record (SEC Rule 204-2) and potentially an all-party-consent problem in CA, IL, FL, WA, PA, MA and others; the Otter.ai privacy litigation survived a motion to dismiss in Aug 2026 on federal wiretap, CIPA §631 and BIPA claims, with CIPA statutory damages of $5,000 per violation. The SEC's FY2027 exam priorities (announced 23 Oct 2026) put adviser AI use squarely in scope, and exam document requests already ask firms to describe AI used in client service, produce AI policies, and show supervision evidence. What small firms actually do today: a written policy nobody can verify, an advisor eyeballing the participant list, and a spreadsheet of "approved tools". No admin console gives them the answer — Google's Meet log shows a bot's display name (changeable, unattributable), Teams' external-bot detection is explicitly imperfect, Zoom's dashboard only covers Marketplace apps, and none of them tie bot attendance to consent or to the client it concerned.
target_customer: Chief Compliance Officer (often the COO or a fractional CCO) at an SEC-registered RIA with 5-50 staff and under $1B AUM — 10,500+ SEC-registered firms sit under $1B. Buyer is the CCO; budget already exists for compliance software and exam-prep consulting. Secondary: 20-100 attorney law firms where the IT/risk director owns the same problem.
why_now: Three things changed in the last 12 months. (1) The Otter.ai privacy litigation order (Aug 2026) let federal wiretap, California CIPA §631 and Illinois BIPA claims proceed against a notetaker vendor on the theory that it was an independent eavesdropper — turning "a bot sat in" from an annoyance into quantified legal exposure ($5,000/violation under CIPA §637.2; $1,000-$5,000 under BIPA). (2) The SEC announced FY2027 examination priorities on 23 Oct 2026 with explicit focus on adviser AI use, and consultants are already circulating 20-item AI exam document request lists. (3) The capability side: Google Admin SDK Reports API (Meet log events) and Microsoft Graph callRecords (CallRecords.Read.All, 30-day retention) now let a tenant-authorised third-party app reconstruct who actually joined each meeting — and Claude Meetings' launch on 12 Nov 2026 (81k likes) signals that first-party AI participants are about to arrive in every call, multiplying the problem. Investor signals weighed: a16z "AI will finally upgrade banking and insurance infrastructure" (Angela Strange, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/) and "Vertical AI evolves... to multiplayer" (Alex Immerman, same link); YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert) describes exactly the solo-CCO buyer who needs tooling to act like a specialist.
comparables: Zocks (zocks.io) — advisor-focused, documents consent status per client/meeting with a read-only change history, and deliberately does not record audio/video; strong on consent for its OWN capture, nothing on third-party bots that join. Jump (jump.ai) — detects verbal consent in its transcript and can require staff attestation; again only for meetings Jump itself is in. Avoma, Fellow — consent enforcement levels, accept/decline, audit logs, Global Relay integration; same limitation: they govern their own bot. Otter, Fireflies Enterprise — admin controls over their own notetaker, not rivals'. Notetaker Guard (The Flow Partners, on AWS Marketplace at $21.99 per protected meeting user/12-month term, and Zoom Marketplace) — the closest direct competitor: real-time bot detection across Zoom/Teams/Meet with audit logs. It appears early-stage, is sold as a security/IT product, and nothing in its listings shows consent evidence capture or an RIA exam-ready output. Nudge Security, Synk.to, Jazz Security — shadow-AI discovery at the identity-provider layer; they find which employees authorised which notetaker app, not what happened in a given client meeting. Native platforms — Google Meet logs give a changeable display name, Microsoft warns its external-bot detection is imperfect, Zoom's bot dashboard only covers Marketplace apps. The gap: nobody joins "which bot was in this specific client meeting" to "did the client consent" to "here is the record an examiner can read" for the small regulated firm.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. 10,500+ SEC-registered advisers under $1B AUM (SEC 2025 adviser statistics) plus state-registered firms and thousands of mid-size law firms. Comparable spend that is documented: Global Relay archiving reported around $15/user/month with a 10-user minimum and $995 setup; Smarsh roughly $8-$35/user/month with a reported $25k annual platform minimum for Cloud Capture; one RIA compliance platform lists $199/$699/$1,499 per month tiers; AI-governance consultants publish $9,500 framework and $17,500 "SEC exam-ready" packages. A $300-$900/month seat-light product for a 15-person RIA sits comfortably inside that band. Even 500 firms at $500/month is $3M ARR — a real business, not a venture-scale one until it expands to law firms, accounting and healthcare, where the same consent-and-evidence job exists.
risks: 1. The pain is real but the urgency is still diffuse: my research found no SEC deficiency letter or FINRA exam item that asks "who recorded this call," and no verified client DDQ clause demanding a no-AI-recording attestation. The buyer may defer until an examiner or a client actually asks. 2. Platform dependency and detection quality — Microsoft itself says bot detection is imperfect, bots can join under generic accounts, and botless desktop recorders never appear in the roster at all, so Bouncer can be defeated and must be honest about coverage. 3. Encroachment: Zocks and Jump already own the RIA meeting-consent relationship and could add third-party bot detection as a feature; Zoom/Google could ship native bot admission logs and shrink the wedge.
riskiest_assumptions: 1. That a sub-$1B RIA CCO will pay for evidence of a risk no examiner has yet cited to them — i.e. that this is a budgeted purchase in 2026/27, not a 2028 purchase after the first enforcement action. 2. That admin-API data (Google Admin SDK Meet log events, Microsoft Graph callRecords, Zoom bot dashboard) is reliable enough to name the bot and attribute it to a person, given changeable display names and botless recorders. 3. That the CCO, not IT, owns this and will grant tenant-wide admin consent (CallRecords.Read.All is broad) to a two-person startup.
first_customers: (a) Fractional/outsourced CCO firms serving 10-40 RIAs each — one sale installs across a book; find them through RIA Compliance Consultants' webinar audience, the NSCP member list and Kitces-adjacent LinkedIn circles. (b) Sub-$1B RIAs in all-party-consent states (California, Illinois, Washington, Massachusetts, Florida) who already circulated an AI notetaker policy this year — searchable from firm ADV Part 2 and LinkedIn posts. (c) Compliance consultants publishing AI exam-prep content (Fairview's "20 AI Questions SEC Exams," workwisesolutions' $9,500/$17,500 packages) — they are selling the problem already and need a tool to deliver against it. (d) 20-100 attorney law firms whose MSP (e.g. Uptime Legal, which publishes on removing uninvited notetakers) is fielding the question.
validation_test: This week: email 25 CCOs at sub-$1B RIAs and 5 fractional-CCO firms with one question and one offer — "Can you tell me, for last month, which AI notetakers joined your client meetings and whether the client consented? If not, I'll run a free one-off Meeting Bot Audit on your Google Workspace or Zoom tenant and send you a PDF." Pass: 5+ grant read-only admin access within 10 days, and 2+ say they'd pay $300-$900/month for it standing, in writing. Fail: fewer than 3 grant access, or everyone says "our policy covers it" without wanting the report — that means latent, not urgent, and this becomes a feature Zocks adds.
build_plan: Narrowest first version, sellable as a standing monthly report before the real-time product exists. 1) Read-only tenant connector: Google Admin SDK Reports API (Meet log events) and Zoom's bot/app dashboard + Calendar API. Skip Teams in v1 — CallRecords.Read.All is a tenant-wide permission that will stall deals with cautious firms. 2) Bot fingerprint library: a maintained list of the ~50 named notetaker vendors (display-name patterns, join behaviour, OAuth client IDs) matched against each meeting's participant roster, plus an "unidentified non-human participant" bucket you report honestly rather than guess at. 3) Per-meeting evidence record: meeting, advisor, client/external domains, bot name + vendor + match confidence, join/leave times, who in the tenant authorised that vendor's OAuth app, whether a consent artefact exists, and a free-text attestation field the advisor completes in one click from an email. 4) The monthly Exam Pack: a PDF/CSV covering every client meeting — approved bot, unapproved bot, client-side bot, no bot — with exceptions ranked, mapped to the firm's own AI policy. This is the sellable artefact. 5) Exception workflow: Slack/email alert within 24h when an unapproved or client-side bot attends, with a pre-written deletion-request template. Cut from v1: real-time admission/blocking, Teams, botless desktop-recorder detection, any transcript storage or processing (never touch content — it's a liability and it's the incumbents' job), and any claim of legal compliance. Price $400/month flat up to 25 staff; sell through fractional-CCO firms.
reasoning: This beat the other candidates because it is the only one where a named buyer with an existing compliance budget faces a change that is dated and documented (Otter litigation order Aug 2026; SEC FY2027 priorities 23 Oct 2026) and where I could show, from incumbents' own documentation, exactly who is left out: every consent tool on the market governs only its own bot, so the client's bot and the unapproved bot go unrecorded. It builds on no past idea — the library's closest neighbours are SkillProof (approval layer for agent skills, engineering buyer) and Driftwatch (vendor surface drift, platform teams); Bouncer serves a compliance officer at a regulated financial firm with a meeting-evidence workflow, a different buyer and a different artefact. Honest limits, which is why this is a 6.8 and a watch, not a dig_deeper: the wedge is structurally weak. Detection can be defeated by renamed bots and botless recorders, Microsoft admits its own detection is imperfect, and the product needs tenant-wide admin consent from a cautious buyer — that is a months-long build and a slow first sale, not a weeks-long one. And the pain is only half-expressed: lawyers and compliance consultants write about it constantly, but I could not verify a single SEC deficiency letter or client DDQ that forces the purchase. What would make people notice it: the first SEC deficiency or CIPA class action naming a small advisory firm. If the validation test returns three tenants in ten days, this becomes an 8; if it returns policy-shrugs, it is a feature Zocks ships next quarter.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Bouncer — meeting-bot control + consent evidence for RIAs/law firms (PICK). Only candidate with a budgeted buyer, a dated regulatory trigger and a provable gap in incumbents' own docs. 2. Claude Meetings artefact-to-system-of-record bridge (push whiteboards/docs generated in-call into Jira/CRM) — dropped at screen: Anthropic will own this, and it's a feature. 3. Privileged-meeting mode for law firms (block all capture, issue a signed no-recording certificate) — finalist; folded into Bouncer as the legal-vertical expansion, since the buyer is an IT director with no standing budget line and the artefact is the same. 4. DFM-feedback-in-minutes for hardware startups buying CNC parts (from twentyfour26) — finalist; dropped at critique: CloudNC Quote Agent, Paperless Parts, DigiFabster, Xometry and Protolabs all serve this with instant DFM, and the library already holds Sidecar, Outbound, Promiseline and Dockside in adjacent machine-shop workflows. 5. Agent-approval mobile inbox for non-developer ops teams (from DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish) — dropped at screen: no buyer outside engineering yet, and it's a feature of every agent platform. 6. Editor/IDE extension allowlist-and-attestation for regulated engineering orgs (from Jack Cable's guide) — dropped as too close to the library's SkillProof and Blastdoor, same buyer and same approve/deny workflow. 7. Package-cooldown enforcement as a managed service for CTOs (7-day minimum package age) — dropped: library already has Freshline and Strangers on this exact material. 8. Location/context-triggered compliance nudges for field workers in trades and home health (from the Instinct reminders post) — dropped at screen: latent pain, no named buyer, consumer-shaped. 9. Micro-SIP onboarding rails for non-Indian emerging markets (from sipsea) — dropped: regulated, licence-heavy, far from this builder's skills and time. 10. Transformer/switchgear expediting for the data-center buildout (YC Data Center Supply Chain signal) — dropped as a near-repeat of Slotkeeper in the library.

PROJECT
1. Blindspot — paste a public repo, map the agent-written files no human has touched since, weekly delta. PICK: a real question people are asking this month (Osmani's essay), every comparable is a local CLI, fully static build, confirmed dependencies.
2. Cooldown Lens — paste a repo URL, show which transitive deps are younger than 7 days per Jack Cable's guide. Dropped at screen: too close to past ideas Freshline and Strangers (same lockfile-in, supply-chain-out workflow), and npm-cooldown already does it.
3. Extension Powers — audit your installed VS Code/Cursor extensions for permissions. Dropped at screen: direct repeat of Blastdoor in the library.
4. Skill/MCP risk card — paste your MCP config and get a risk card. Dropped at screen: repeats SkillPeek and SkillProof; mcp-scan and mcp-audit exist and are free.
5. Transcript→Whiteboard — paste a meeting transcript, get an editable Excalidraw/Mermaid diagram (from the Claude Meetings post). Finalist, lost: Mermaid AI does transcript-upload-to-diagram today, Excalidraw converts Mermaid natively, and the output is a generic diagram nobody posts. Also sits uncomfortably close to tonight's venture (meetings).
6. Untangle — paste a repo, get a "tangle score" with cycles and duplication. Finalist, lost: NeedyNodes, CodeFlow and GRASP all do free browser-based dependency maps with cycle and dead-code detection; crowded and the output isn't personal.
7. Repo Quiz — five questions about your own repo, scored. Dropped at screen: Repo Tutor, repo-interview, popquiz and vibecheck all exist, and the quiz format is a chore, not a 10-second result.
8. Agent Session Replay — drop a Claude Code JSONL and watch the session as a timeline. Dropped at screen: agentplay, agentcam, agent-replay and Agent Work Visualizer all shipped in 2026; saturated.
9. Session Stats Card — drop your Claude Code JSONL, get a shareable usage card. Dropped at screen: CodeBurn, Token Battle, viberank, claude-carbon crowd this; and the builder's library already leans on paste-your-config cards.
10. Mac Cluster Playground — a browser visualiser for Apple container's new local Kubernetes clusters. Dropped at generate: audience is tiny, there's no input the user already has, and it needs a Mac-local backend.
11. Chore Recency tracker (from the laundry-reminder post). Dropped at screen: lastGLANCE, SinceNow and a dozen apps do it; nothing new makes it possible.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Claude Meetings (what it produces, Team/Enterprise rollout, Google Meet only), twentyfour26 + the on-demand CNC landscape (Xometry/Protolabs/Fictiv lead times and the ~$65 Protolabs starting price), and Jack Cable's Nov 2026 security guide plus Addy Osmani's "cognitive surrender" article. These killed candidates 4 and 6 early — the CNC DFM space is well served and the extension-governance space duplicates the library. Screening pot (6/6): checked AI-notetaker consent law, CNC quoting incumbents, IDE extension governance, benefits-eligibility verification (SteadyIQ already there), FINRA/SEC archiving, and shadow-AI meeting-bot detection. The notetaker checks were the only ones that returned a live, unserved workflow. Deep research (12/12): mapped the incumbent consent tooling (Zocks, Jump, Avoma, Fellow, Otter, Fireflies), found the one direct competitor (Notetaker Guard, $21.99/protected-meeting-user/12mo on AWS Marketplace, by The Flow Partners), confirmed the Otter.ai Aug 2026 ruling and CIPA §637.2 / BIPA damages, confirmed SEC FY2027 exam priorities (23 Oct 2026) and the Fairview 20-question AI exam request list, confirmed no cross-platform bot/consent log exists in Google, Microsoft or Zoom admin consoles, and sized the buyer pool (10,500+ SEC advisers under $1B) and adjacent pricing (Global Relay ~$15/user/mo, Smarsh $8-35/user/mo, consultants at $9,500-$17,500). Sharpening pot (5/5): tested the reshaped RIA-CCO version — RIA Compliance Consultants' own slides tell firms to maintain approved-tool inventories and documented per-meeting consent; Cooley confirms transcripts can be books-and-records; Google Admin SDK Reports API and Microsoft Graph callRecords are reachable by tenant-authorised ISVs (so the first version is buildable); but searches for client DDQ attestation clauses and for "who recorded this call" in SEC/FINRA exam items came back empty, which is why pain and wedge stayed capped. Investor signals weighed: a16z Angela Strange (banking/insurance infrastructure) and Alex Immerman (vertical AI goes multiplayer) aimed me at the regulated-financial buyer; YC's "$15-an-Hour Expert" described the solo-CCO persona; I deliberately avoided YC's "AI for City Hall" because the library already holds Backcheck and Condition in the permitting space.
Sharpening (6.2 to 6.8): Round 1 — weakest criteria were market_pull (5: "IT admins" is not a budget line) and gap (6: Notetaker Guard, Nudge, Synk all detect bots). Change: moved the buyer from the enterprise IT/security admin to the CCO at a sub-$1B SEC-registered RIA, and moved the wedge from "block bots" to "produce the consent-and-attendance evidence record." Research (RIA Compliance Consultants slide deck, Fairview's 20 AI exam questions, Cooley on notetakers and the books-and-records rule, SEC FY2027 priorities, Zocks/Jump/Avoma/Fellow consent docs) confirmed: regulators are asking advisers to evidence AI use and supervision; every incumbent consent tool only governs its own bot, leaving third-party and client-side bots undocumented; and 10,500+ SEC advisers sit under $1B. market_pull 5→7, gap 6→7, pain 6→7, timing 7→8. Round 2 — tried to lift wedge by testing whether the data is actually reachable without a huge build: Google Admin SDK Reports API (Meet log events) and Microsoft Graph callRecords are available to tenant-authorised third-party apps, which makes a read-only "Meeting Bot Audit" report shippable as a first version. But the same research showed display names are changeable, Microsoft calls its own detection imperfect, callRecords retains only 30 days, and botless desktop recorders never appear in the roster — so the first version can honestly report "a bot named X joined" but not reliably attribute or guarantee coverage. That caps the wedge: wedge stayed 5 rather than rising. I also searched for client-side DDQ clauses demanding no-AI-recording attestations and for SEC deficiency letters asking "who recorded this call"; neither was verifiable, so I did not raise pain above 7. Average 6.2 → 6.8.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Apple container 1.7.1's new local Kubernetes clusters (interesting, but no consumer input — killed candidate 10); Addy Osmani's Nov 3 X essay, which turned out to be the cognitive-surrender argument with no new data of its own but 21k likes, and became the spine of the pick; and Jack Cable's security guide, which gave the concrete 7-day cooldown advice behind candidate 2 (later dropped as a library repeat).

Screening pot (5/5): one search each on AI-code comprehension quizzes (thin, no hosted winner), Instinct-style location reminders (crowded personal-agent space), untangle/codebase smell tools (crowded), transcript-to-diagram (Mermaid AI exists), and chore-recency apps (lastGLANCE, SinceNow — dead). These five kills are what cleared the field down to three finalists.

Deep research pot (8/8): confirmed GitDiagram/Gitingest/Emerge cover architecture maps but not smell scores; confirmed NeedyNodes, CodeFlow and GRASP already do free browser dependency maps with cycles and dead code, which killed Untangle; confirmed Mermaid AI does transcript→diagram, which killed the whiteboard idea; found fragility, cdebt, git-pulse, cocommit and popquiz as the real comparables for Blindspot and established that all are local CLIs; confirmed npm registry and deps.dev access from the browser (used to rule the cooldown ideas out as repeats rather than as infeasible); confirmed GitHub unauthenticated CORS access and the 60/hr limit; and checked Gemini 3 Flash / Claude Haiku 4.5 pricing — which mattered because it let me cut the LLM from the build entirely, making Blindspot a pure static page.

Sharpening pot (4/4): verified the commits endpoint returns full messages with trailers at 100 per page unauthenticated (the mechanism the whole tool rests on); verified html2canvas can make the share card client-side with no backend and that Vercel OG would need a server, so the card is a download rather than an og:image; searched for an existing paste-a-URL AI-authorship map with a shareable card and found only local tools (Project MRI, git-ai, AgentPrint); and read the Nov 2026 arXiv work on detecting agent commits (7.84M commits, AUC up to 0.859 but precision ≤0.332), which directly changed the design — I dropped any plan to infer unmarked agent commits heuristically and made the tool honest about measuring *marked* commits only, with "days since a human touched it" as the second, independent axis.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: you look at your repo's agent share once and never return). Change: added the weekly trend — the score is stored per repo with a date, the page draws a 5-week sparkline and names the *new* blind spots since last week, so the thing you come back for is the delta, not the number. Research (deep pot, prior-art calls on fragility/cdebt/git-pulse/bus-factor tools) found every comparable is a one-shot local CLI run; none tracks the score over time and none is hosted. Usefulness 5 → 7 (capped below 8 because I have no evidence people actually return to a repo-health score weekly; that's assumption (c)). Score 7.2 → 7.6.
Round 2 — weakest remaining: shareability (7, "shareable with effort" — a treemap of your own repo's weaknesses is not obviously postable). Change: reframed the headline so it cuts both ways — the card leads with the single percentage and the three worst files, which makes it a confession *or* a flex ("87% human-reviewed"), and the launch move is to publish maps of five well-known OSS repos first so people paste their own in reply. Research (sharpening pot) confirmed GitHub's commits endpoint returns full messages with trailers unauthenticated and CORS-enabled (60 req/hr/IP), and that html2canvas can produce the PNG fully client-side with no backend — so the card is real, not aspirational; also confirmed buildability at 9 (static page, zero API cost). Shareability 7 → 8, buildability 8 → 9. Score 7.6 → 8.0. I did not raise wow or freshness: nothing new appeared to justify it.
prototype_summary: An interactive Bouncer prototype that turns a messy, unattributable meeting participant log into a named, attested exception list and a generated October 2026 Exam Pack document for a fictional SEC-registered RIA.
